rv.q: If this production lacks the teeming, motley exuberance that pulses in Ibsen's text, it definitely distills the intriguing philosophical essence of a play that still seems unsettlingly relevant.

Mr. Doyle’s staging, by contrast, struck me as almost penitentially drab, denuded of much of the play’s humor and stripped of Edvard Grieg’s justly popular incidental music (which in this country is far better known than the play itself).
It will not be to everyone’s liking.
In the case of PEER GYNT, there’s so much oxygen in the room that it has displaced other key elements needed for an evening of engaging theater, such as a sense of place and emotional resonance.
This Peer Gynt wanders, confusingly, through a series of episodes that lead nowhere.
This hapless hybrid of Cirque and the Great White Way does something unexpected: it makes you want to run away and not join the circus.
Unfortunately, the remainder of this cleverly conceived but confusingly executed production is as sleepy as it is opaque.
All the more reason, then, to relish the admirable, absorbing production of Peer Gynt now playing at Classic Stage Company.
Ibsen’s “Peer Gynt” restores the hope that these three things might abide and restore our wounded hearts and disillusioned selves.

As it stands, it’s a production admirable for its economy, excellent performances and ambitious direction, but just like its central character it can’t help but alienate others who’d rather move on than indulge its narcissism.
However, in the case of this production, more might have been more.
Without that, and in spite of Ebert’s great efforts, the play seems irrelevant … even silly.
Everything about Doyle’s production is dark.
Like that onion, this peeled-back Peer Gynt is hollow at the core.

cn.t: Doyle's stripped-down adaptation of Ibsen's epic divides critics: some praise the minimalist approach and strong cast, but most find it dramatically inert and overlong, with the condensed version losing the play's pageantry and emotional impact.
